name: Translation and the Planned Fade
title: Translation and the Planned Fade
answer: Live translation lets a newcomer follow a lesson from the first day, but the support should be planned to fade as English grows. Teachers and English language development specialists decide together how that support decreases over time, and any machine translation of academic content needs a bilingual reviewer before it becomes a lasting resource.

sections.body: Live translation tools such as Microsoft Translator can show a teacher's spoken words as text in a student's own language, so a newcomer can take part in class right away rather than waiting until enough English is in place. The problem this solves is the gap between a student's knowledge and their current English, which otherwise keeps them out of lessons for months. At the same time, support that never changes can hold a student back, because relying on translation for every lesson in the second year may slow the building of English. The idea is therefore two sided: give the support early, then plan its gradual removal in step with each student's growth. The teacher and the English language development specialist share the job of deciding how that decrease happens.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a teacher can run live translation during instruction so a newcomer reads the lesson in their own language while hearing it in English. The book describes this support as appropriate from the first day and notes that secondary school students used machine translation flexibly and thoughtfully at every stage of learning English, choosing for themselves when to lean on it and when to work in English. Over time the teacher and the English language development specialist plan how the support decreases, keeping the fade gradual and matched to what each student can now do. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond its focus on secondary schools and newcomers. Any translated academic material that is meant to last should pass a bilingual reviewer first.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. It cites Kelly (2021), research in secondary schools finding that English learners used machine translation flexibly and thoughtfully at every stage of learning English, choosing when to rely on it and when to work in English. On the quality of machine translation, it cites Dew et al. (2018), research in health care finding that machine translation works best on simple sentences and in widely spoken European languages and should be treated as a first draft. It also cites Strechen et al. (2025), a review of 18 studies that found serious errors in a majority of them, with accuracy lower for languages such as Haitian Creole and Vietnamese. Academic terms, idioms, and subject specific meanings are especially likely to go wrong.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Machine translation of academic content should not become a lasting resource until a bilingual reviewer has checked it, because it is best treated as a first draft and serious errors appeared in a majority of the studies reviewed, with weaker accuracy for languages such as Haitian Creole and Vietnamese. Academic terms, idioms, and subject specific meanings are the most likely to fail. Translation support should fade as English grows, and a student who leans on it for every lesson in the second year may not build English as fast as they could. The decisions about how and when support decreases stay with people, namely the teacher and the English language development specialist, who plan the fade gradually and match it to each student's growth.
